FDA’s categories list (updated 14 May 2026) does not place it in Category 1, 2 or 3.

Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (23 July 2026). FDA’s Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) considered BPC-157 (free base) and BPC-157 acetate for the 503A Bulks List on 23 July 2026. In its briefing document, FDA proposed that neither form be included. FDA has not posted minutes or vote results on the meeting page, and this page gives no vote counts. The HHS policy’s Appendix B states that “Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER) recommended against listing either form, and the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) voted in favor of inclusion.” Advisory committee recommendations are non-binding.

Draft interim policy published for comment (announced 28 October 2026). The HHS Office of the Secretary filed a Federal Register notice of availability (FR Doc. 2026-22192; Docket No. HHS-OASH-2026-0496; RIN 0910-ZD94) for a draft “Enforcement Discretion Policy Regarding 503A Compounding Using Certain Peptide Bulk Drug Substances”. The notice is scheduled for publication on 30 October 2026, and it states that written comments can be submitted “until 2 weeks after date of publication in the Federal Register”. OIRA concluded its review on 27 October 2026. BPC-157 is one of six peptides in the policy’s Appendix A. The policy states that, until a peptide “is addressed in a final rule as being included or not included on the 503A bulks list,” HHS “does not intend to take action against a State licensed pharmacy, Federal facility, or licensed physician” compounding with it “when all of the following circumstances are present”.

Scope: the identity listed in Appendix B is BPC-157 acetate only, for “subcutaneous, intramuscular, oral, and topical dosage forms”, with the amino acid sequence Gly-Glu-Pro-Pro-Pro-Gly-Lys-Pro-Ala-Asp-Asp-Ala-Gly-Leu-Val. Other forms, including BPC-157 free base, are outside the listed identity. The compounded product may contain only a single active ingredient, so blends are outside the policy. For oral forms the compounder is expected to keep documentation of adequate oral bioavailability in humans. This describes the policy’s scope. It is not usage guidance.

Conditions (summary): the bulk substance must come from a facility registered under section 510 with a valid certificate of analysis (COA) whose test results meet the testing standard in Appendix B; the original manufacturer must be FDA-registered and CGMP-compliant, with its location on the certificate; compounders must report products compounded, serious adverse events and product quality issues to FDA and to the States, and serious adverse events and product quality issues to FDA’s MedWatch program; the label must state “This is a compounded drug product. Not for resale.”; the only co-packaged device may be an FDA 510(k)-cleared syringe; and section 503A’s insanitary-conditions and patient-specific prescription requirements still apply.

Not an approval: the notice states that “Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, which means FDA does not review their safety, effectiveness, or quality before they are marketed.” The policy makes no safety or efficacy finding for BPC-157.

Not a Bulks List listing and not Category 1: BPC-157 is not on the 503A Bulks List (21 CFR 216.23(a)) and is not in any FDA interim category. The notice says FDA’s future rulemakings “may propose adding some or all of these peptides” to the list; no such proposed rule has been published.

Interim and non-binding: there is no calendar end date. The policy applies until a final rule addresses each peptide, HHS “may revisit” it “if, among other things, a safety signal or product quality issue arises”, and the notice says it “is not binding on HHS or the public.”

Research-use-only products: HHS describes the policy as meant to “discourage the continued, widespread use of certain research-use-only peptides supplied by foreign manufacturers that pose a safety risk to US patients.” Nothing in the policy treats research-use-only products as covered.

Other status lines are unchanged: on FDA’s "Certain Bulk Drug Substances for Use in Compounding that May Present Significant Safety Risks" page, BPC-157 is listed as nominated but withdrawn. BPC-157 remains on WADA’s S0 (non-approved substances) list.

WADA has banned BPC-157 for athletes under the class of "S0: Non-approved substances." This means athletes can face sanctions if caught using it in sport. The ban signals that BPC-157 is considered experimental and not recognized as a legitimate medication.
One attractive feature of BPC-157 in research is its apparently favorable safety profile in animals. Toxicology studies have found no lethal dose even at extremely high amounts:
In rats, a single injection of 20 mg per kilogram (a massive dose for a peptide) caused no deaths or obvious toxic effects
In dogs, daily injections for a month at doses up to 1 mg/kg showed no significant adverse effects compared to control animals
Studies reported no changes in body weight, behavior, or organ health attributable to BPC-157

The most prominent theoretical concern is BPC-157's ability to promote growth factors and blood vessel formation. While beneficial for healing injuries, this raises a question: could BPC-157 unintentionally help existing cancer cells grow or spread? Cancerous tumors often exploit the same pathways (like FAK/paxillin and VEGF) to invade tissues and nourish themselves with blood supply.

This idea is currently theoretical – no study has shown BPC-157 causes cancer in animals or humans. In fact, one lab test showed BPC-157 inhibited growth of a particular cancer cell line in culture. Nonetheless, experts urge caution until more is known about long-term effects.

NSW Health reported (19 Oct 2026) 1,180 presentations to NSW emergency departments associated with peptide use between 1 July 2025 and 30 September 2026. The release does not break this figure down by peptide. The release names BPC-157 among the peptides that products may claim to contain and states: "None of these peptides are currently approved in Australia for any purpose." The release also says that when a patient with serious illness likely due to peptide use is identified, NSW Health works with the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA), and where relevant, law enforcement agencies, to investigate the source of the product.

expected.title: Pilot Safety Studies

entries.value:
To date, only minimal human testing has been published. A 2025 pilot study (Lee and Burgess, Alternative Therapies in Health and Medicine; PMID 40131143), carried out at a private clinic in Florida, gave BPC-157 by intravenous infusion on two consecutive days to two adults who had received intravenous BPC-157 before. The authors reported no side effects and no measurable changes in the tested heart, liver, kidney, thyroid and blood glucose markers.

With two participants, no control group and three days of follow-up, the study cannot establish safety. FDA’s July 2026 briefing document for its Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee notes that the published human studies of BPC-157 were of short duration, had small sample sizes and gave limited information on safety.

expected.title: Registered Phase 1 Trial Without Published Results

entries.value: A Phase 1 study in healthy volunteers, PCO-02 (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02637284, sponsor PharmaCotherapia), was registered in December 2015 to assess the safety and pharmacokinetics of BPC-157 oral tablets against placebo, with a single-administration part and a two-week repeated-administration part and an estimated enrollment of 42. The registry record was last updated in December 2015, its status is listed as unknown, and no results are posted. FDA’s July 2026 briefing document states that FDA was unable to find an associated published study.

expected.title: Current Status

entries.value: Published human data on BPC-157 are limited to a few small, short studies. Most had no control group; the two placebo-controlled studies FDA identified (rectal enemas in healthy volunteers and in people with ulcerative colitis) are available only as meeting abstracts. A 2026 systematic review (Poolton et al., Acta Orthopaedica Belgica; PMID 42885452) rated the overall certainty of evidence as very low. FDA’s July 2026 briefing document concluded that there is insufficient clinical safety information to characterize the safety profile of BPC-157 (free base) and BPC-157 acetate. Until controlled human trials are published, any human use is experimental.

expected:
"Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence" when it comes to safety. Because BPC-157 has not been extensively studied in people, there could be side effects that haven't been observed in small samples. Minor side effects like headaches, dizziness, or injection site reactions might not show up in tiny studies but could in larger populations.

Regulatory status (as of 29 October 2026): BPC-157 is not approved by FDA and is not on the 503A Bulks List. A July 2026 advisory committee vote is non-binding. A draft interim enforcement-discretion policy published for comment by the HHS Office of the Secretary (FR Doc. 2026-22192) describes when HHS does not intend to take action against 503A compounding of BPC-157 acetate. It is not an approval, has no fixed end date, may be revisited by HHS, and makes no safety or efficacy finding. PeptideMap does not predict outcomes.

To date, only minimal human testing has been published.
